items.question: Which type of muscle is found ONLY in the heart?
items.explanation: Cardiac muscle is found exclusively in the heart. It is cylindrical, branched, uninucleate, involuntary, and contracts rhythmically throughout life. Striated muscle is in limbs; smooth muscle is in alimentary canal and other organs.

items.question: Smooth muscles are called "involuntary" because:

options.B: They cannot be controlled consciously by our will
options.D: They are found only in the heart

items.explanation: Smooth muscles are called involuntary because they work automatically, without conscious control. The movement of food in the alimentary canal and constriction of blood vessels happen without us thinking about it. We cannot start or stop these movements by will.

items.question: A student observes a muscle tissue slide showing: cylindrical cells, branched, one nucleus per cell, striations visible. What type of muscle is this?
items.explanation: Cardiac muscle has cylindrical, branched, uninucleate cells with striations. This combination uniquely identifies cardiac muscle. Striated/skeletal muscle is unbranched and multinucleate; smooth muscle is spindle-shaped with no striations.

items.question: Which statement about smooth muscle is INCORRECT?

options.C: Found in the iris of the eye and alimentary canal

items.explanation: Smooth muscle is INVOLUNTARY - it is NOT under conscious control. It works automatically (e.g., food movement in gut, iris adjustment to light). Options A, B, and C are all correct descriptions of smooth muscle.

items.question: Contractile proteins in muscle fibres are responsible for:

options.C: Contracting and relaxing to cause movement

items.explanation: Muscle fibres contain special proteins called contractile proteins (actin and myosin). When these proteins interact, they cause the muscle fibre to shorten (contract) and then return to original length (relax), producing movement. Options A, B, D describe functions of nervous, glandular, and blood tissues respectively.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: All cells possess the ability to respond to stimuli, but cells of nervous tissue are highly specialised for being stimulated and transmitting stimuli very rapidly.
Brain, spinal cord, and nerves are all composed of nervous tissue.
NEURON (NERVE CELL): the functional unit.
CELL BODY: large nucleus + cytoplasm. From it arise long thin hair-like parts (processes).
AXON: usually one long part per neuron; transmits impulse AWAY from cell body; may be up to a metre long.
DENDRITES: many short, branched parts; RECEIVE stimuli; carry impulses TOWARD cell body.
NERVE ENDING: end of axon; connects to next neuron or effector (muscle/gland) through a junction called synapse.
NERVE IMPULSE: the signal (electrical signal) that passes along the nerve fibre. Nerve impulses allow us to move our muscles when we want to and allow the body to react rapidly to stimuli.
NERVE: many nerve fibres bound together by connective tissue make up a nerve.
The functional combination of nerve and muscle tissue is fundamental to most animals - enables rapid movement in response to stimuli.

items.question: What is a nerve impulse?
items.answer: A nerve impulse is the signal (electrical signal) that passes along the nerve fibre. It allows neurons to transmit information rapidly from one part of the body to another. Nerve impulses allow us to move our muscles and respond to stimuli in the environment.

items.question: What is the function of dendrites in a neuron?
items.answer: Dendrites are the short, branched parts of the neuron that arise from the cell body. They receive stimuli (signals) from the environment or from other neurons and carry the nerve impulse toward the cell body. From the cell body, the impulse is then transmitted along the axon.

items.question: Describe the structure of a neuron in detail.
items.answer:
A neuron (nerve cell) has three main parts:

1. CELL BODY (SOMA):
- Largest part of the neuron.
- Contains a large nucleus and cytoplasm.
- Many long thin hair-like processes (extensions) arise from it.

2. DENDRITES:
- Many short, branched parts arising from the cell body.
- Receive stimuli and carry impulses TOWARD the cell body.
- Increase the surface area for receiving signals.

3. AXON:
- Usually each neuron has a single, long axon.
- Carries nerve impulses AWAY from the cell body to the next neuron or effector (muscle or gland).
- An individual nerve cell (axon) may be up to a metre long.
- At the end is the NERVE ENDING which connects to the next neuron through a SYNAPSE.

Additional:
- MYELIN SHEATH: in many neurons, the axon is covered by a fatty myelin sheath for insulation and faster impulse conduction.
- Many nerve fibres bound together by connective tissue = a NERVE.

items.question: The functional unit of nervous tissue is:
items.explanation: The neuron (nerve cell) is the functional unit of nervous tissue. Each neuron consists of a cell body, axon, and dendrites. An axon and dendrite are parts of a neuron; a nerve is made of many nerve fibres (axons) bound together.

items.question: Nerve impulses are carried AWAY from the cell body by:
items.explanation: The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body toward the next neuron or effector organ (muscle/gland). Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body. The synapse is the junction between two neurons.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of a neuron?
items.explanation: A sarcomere is the functional unit of muscle fibres (contractile unit in striated muscle), not a part of neurons. A neuron consists of cell body (soma), axon, and dendrites.

items.question: A student claims: "Since neurons can be up to a metre long, they must be the largest cells in the body." Which statement correctly evaluates this?

options.A: Correct; neurons are the largest cells in every way
options.B: Partially correct; neurons can have very long axons (up to a metre) making them among the longest cells, but cell size refers to various dimensions and the cell body of a neuron is not necessarily the largest
options.C: Incorrect; neurons are the smallest cells in the body
options.D: Incorrect; nerve impulses travel in the axon but the axon is not part of the cell

items.explanation: Neurons can indeed have axons up to a metre long (e.g., nerve cells in the sciatic nerve), making them among the longest cells in the body. However, "largest" in terms of volume or cell body size is not necessarily the neuron. The axon is definitely a part of the neuron cell (D wrong). Neurons are not the smallest cells (C wrong).

items.question: Brain, spinal cord, and nerves are all composed of:
items.explanation: The brain, spinal cord, and nerves are all composed of nervous tissue (neurons and supporting cells). Nervous tissue receives, integrates, and transmits information throughout the body. Muscular tissue is responsible for movement; epithelial tissue covers body surfaces; connective tissue connects and supports.
